articles.title: What does the UK-EU ‘reset’ deal mean for immigration and tuition fees?
articles.author: Alan Manning, Professor of Economics, London School of Economics and Political Science
paras: Much of the UK-EU “reset” talks, held in Brussels on November 20, were on the issue of migration. The newly announced measures largely centre on young people and students, with deals hinging on an EU demand to reduce tuition fees for EU students at UK universities. The newly struck deals also mention irregular migration, including channel crossings.

The biggest questions – a return to free movement, the single market or the customs union – are still off the table, but the talks mark a closer post-Brexit relationship between the UK and the EU on migration. So where are we likely to see changes?

First and foremost is the Youth Experience Scheme (YES), which will allow up to 100,000 young people a year to migrate between the UK and EU to work or study for up to three years. The scheme will not be rolled out immediately, and is expected to take effect between 2028 and 2030.
In practice, this will probably be similar to the UK’s current agreements with some non-EU countries, including New Zealand and Canada.

The UK’s schemes with these other countries only use around 25% of their capped numbers, but the cap on the EU scheme will likely be met. This will, of course, raise EU immigration into the UK. But it does not mean 100,000 new arrivals – some coming on the new scheme could previously have come via other channels.
The scheme will also raise UK emigration to EU countries, as some young British people will use the scheme to go to work in the EU. This will limit the overall effect on net migration.
Under the new rules, youth mobility could reach something close to an equilibrium, with a comparable number entering and exiting every year. The impact on net migration could therefore be very small.

The issue of university tuition fees proved to be a sticking point in the negotiations. The EU wants UK and EU students to both pay the same fees as home students – currently £9,790 per year in the UK. A six-month period has been given for these negotiations to be finalised.

The UK may be reluctant because lower tuition fees for EU citizens would prove unpopular among UK universities. While universities widely criticised the rise in EU student fees immediately after the Brexit vote, they have now come to depend on the extra cash.

In July 2026, Vivienne Stern, the CEO of Universities UK, an industry body for UK universities, stated that giving EU students home fee status would now worsen the financial situation for UK universities.

During the Brexit campaign, the “Vote Leave, take back control” slogan promised more control over borders. The Leave campaign argued that EU free movement gave the UK no say over how many EU migrants arrived.

But an irony of Brexit is that it gave the UK less control over asylum claims, including those of people crossing the English Channel in small boats. This was largely because Brexit made UK-EU cooperation harder.
Asylum claims rose from about 40,000 a year pre-pandemic to 100,000 afterwards. In 2019, 1,800 people reach the UK via small boat crossings. The number rose to over 45,000 in 2022.

Although Channel crossings would likely have risen even if the UK had stayed in the EU, Brexit probably reduced control over irregular migration and asylum claims. After Brexit, the UK lost access to the Dublin convention on returns, and with it, the Eurodac asylum database.
This meant cooperation with European countries was no longer automatic, and made the UK a de facto appeals court for asylum-seekers whose EU claims had failed.

Eurodac allows authorities to check asylum seekers’ previous claims and criminal records, and to identify those who had previously applied within the EU. UK authorities have stated that they would like to regain access to Eurodac.

The summit’s joint statement specifically mentions the EU’s Channel Action Plan to tackle dangerous crossings of the English Channel, which the UK joined in July 2026. There were also commitments to a “Structured Dialogue on migration”. All of this is in keeping with the UK government’s efforts to “restore order and control to our borders”.

But this aspect of migration – by far the most politicised among the British electorate – will be the hardest to rein in. Access to Eurodac is complicated, and cannot be solved with one quick summit. Brexit may therefore leave the UK with reduced control over the area of migration where voters want it most.
Alan Manning receives funding from ESRC through the Centre for Economic Performance at LSE. He is a member of the Labour Party

articles.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
articles.author: Martin Steven, Senior Lecturer, School of Global Affairs, Lancaster University
paras: Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.
Burnham is walking a fine line

Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.
At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

articles.title: Independent, Gen Z and Latino voters helped deliver a Democratic wave in 2026 – but that doesn’t mean a lasting realignment
articles.author: Thom Reilly, Professor and Co-Director of the Center for an Independent and Sustainable Democracy; School of Public Affairs, Arizona State University
paras: The Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections raises an important question about American politics. Are independent, Gen Z and Latino voters building a new Democratic coalition, or are they sending a warning to both parties that their support cannot be taken for granted?
The preliminary evidence suggests something more complicated.

Our analysis, including a deep dive into the 2026 Voter Poll conducted by the market research firm SSRS, points to three factors behind the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories: a substantial shift among independent voters toward Democratic candidates, stronger Democratic turnout relative to Republicans, and declining enthusiasm among voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024.
Gen Z, who are people born from 1997 to 2012, and Latino voters played important roles in these shifts.

But the results should not automatically be interpreted as a lasting Democratic realignment. These voters may be demonstrating a willingness to reconsider their political choices when governing parties fail to meet their expectations.

The overlapping influence of independent, younger and Latino voters helps explain the scale of the Democratic gains. Our analysis, based on voter poll data, suggests that independents, who made up about one-third of voters, contributed approximately 52% of the Democrats’ national popular vote margin in House races. Latino voters contributed an estimated 23% of that margin, while voters ages 18 to 29 contributed approximately 39%.
Because these groups overlap, their contributions cannot be added together. But the figures illustrate how important each was to the Democratic advantage.
In our book, “The Independent Voter,” co-authored with Omar Ali, we examine the growing influence of independent voters and their often unpredictable voting behavior.
Independents helped determine the outcome
Independent voters, among the most important contributors to Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to shift between parties.

In 2008, they favored Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama by 8 percentage points. Four years later, they backed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney by 5 points. In the 2016 presidential election, independents favored Republican Trump by 4 points before swinging toward Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, supporting him by 13 points.

In the 2024 presidential election, independents narrowly favored Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump, 49% to 46%. However, Trump performed better among independents in key battleground states, including Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina.
In our research spanning nearly five decades, Dan Hunting and I, Thom Reilly, found that independents exhibit considerably greater volatility in their voting patterns than Democrats and Republicans.

The 3-point advantage independents gave Harris in 2024 provides a useful baseline for understanding their much larger shift toward Democratic candidates in 2026. A November 2026 national survey of more than 90,000 people found that voters identifying with neither major party favored Democratic House candidates by more than 20 percentage points.

Our analysis of voter poll data showed that independents favored House Democrats by 59% to 37%. In addition, independents’ support was consequential in several Republican-held Senate seats that flipped to Democrats, with independent voters providing the margin needed for victory in six of the nine races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina.

The emerging pattern may represent another turn in a longer cycle of electoral volatility among independents. Rather than embracing either party, independent voters appear willing to reconsider their choices as political and economic conditions change.
Did Republicans switch sides or stay home?
There is some disagreement about what produced the midterm Democratic wave.

Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston argue that Republican abstention – those who chose not to vote – was more important nationally than large-scale partisan crossover voting. They report that only approximately 6% of self-identified Republicans voted for Democratic House candidates.
Yet the evidence also demonstrates some crossover voting.
An analysis by the research firm NORC found that approximately 1 in 10 2024 Trump voters in 2026 supported Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina and Texas.
Both dynamics appear to have played a role.

Democrats benefited from stronger participation among their supporters and reduced turnout among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. In several competitive races, Republican defections and strong independent support also contributed to Democratic victories.

Understanding these differences is important. A shift in election results does not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. It may reflect changes in who participates. The 2026 results suggest that both factors were at work.
Younger voters shifted sharply toward Democrats
Gen Z voters were another important part of the Democratic gains.

In 2026, 66% of voters ages 18–29 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 30% who backed Republicans. That 36-point Democratic advantage was substantially larger than the 14-point margin in 2024, according to Tufts University.

There was also evidence of voters switching party choices. Among young people who voted for Trump in 2024 and participated in the 2026 election, 16% supported a Democratic House candidate. And 67% of young voters disapproved of Trump’s performance as president in 2026.
Gallup found that 56% of Gen Z adults identify as political independents, underscoring the weaker ties many younger Americans have to the two major parties.

Combined with economic dissatisfaction and distrust of political institutions, this suggests that younger voters may be especially willing to reconsider their choices when the party in power fails to meet their expectations or deliver on its promises.
Latino voters also shifted substantially
Latino voters showed a similar pattern, but with some differences.
More than 6 in 10 Latino voters supported Democratic House candidates in 2026, according to a NORC survey. That reverses much of the Republican gains among these voters in 2024.

There was also evidence of volatility among Latinos. A postelection survey by UnidosUS and BSP Research found that 17% of Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic House candidates in 2026, compared with just 3% of Harris voters who supported Republicans.
Texas offers an example of how these voting groups overlapped.

According to our analysis of the voter poll data, 68% of Latino voters supported Democrat James Talarico, compared with 30% who backed his Republican opponent. Among voters ages 18 to 29, Talarico won 79% to 19%, while independents favored him by 64% to 33%.
Of course, these groups overlap. A voter can be Latino, young and independent, so their contributions cannot simply be added together numerically.
Still, Latinos’ strong support for Talarico illustrates how shifts among these voting groups helped Democrats win in a traditionally Republican state, perhaps shaping a new composite demographic.
A warning for both political parties
The lesson of 2026 may be less about Democratic realignment than about political accountability.
Republicans benefited in 2024 from dissatisfaction with Democratic governance. Two years later, Democrats benefited from dissatisfaction with Republican governance.
Yet the scale of the Democratic victories should not be understated.

Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency – his handling of the economy, the war in Iran, harsh immigration enforcement policies and concerns about corruption – contributed to a sweeping rejection of his administration and Republican leadership at both the federal and state levels. That includes a Congress that many voters believed had failed to hold him accountable.
Even so, neither party should assume that independents, younger voters or Latinos now belong to its camp.

America’s founders recognized the dangers of excessive party loyalty. In his 1796 farewell address, George Washington warned about the divisive influence of political parties and the dangers of placing party allegiance above the public interest.
More than two centuries later, the growing influence of voters with weaker ties to the major parties raises a similar question about the role of political parties in American democracy.
The 2026 election may not signal a lasting political realignment. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable.
For Democrats and Republicans alike, winning an election does not necessarily mean winning voters’ lasting loyalty.

articles.title: Diplomacy, humour and avoidance – what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
articles.author: Sam Friedman, Professor of Sociology, Department of Sociology, London School of Economics and Political Science
paras: Several years ago, the US economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analysed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

The paper was published in the journal Nature in 2022. Last year, a report from the Behavioural Insights Team came to the same conclusions in the UK. Both have since been seized upon by policymakers seeking to boost social mobility in the general population.

But we were puzzled. Not only did this work seem to rely on a speculative understanding of how friendships actually work, but the conclusions fly in the face of decades of sociological research. Specifically, that friendship rests on reciprocity between friends, not one-way transfers.

In our new paper, we investigated this tension via 42 in-depth interviews with people in cross-class friendships in the UK. We found that these friendships can indeed produce “social capital”. That is, more privileged friends often provide financial support or cultural guidance to less privileged friends navigating elite spaces. Yet our research also underlines the limitations of characterising cross-class friendship in this way.

In our interviews, when support tended to flow only one way, it generated feelings of inequality or indebtedness, and often sent friendships into a downward spiral. Take Tania (not her real name), a researcher who was white and from a lower-middle-class background. She met Florence at Durham University, where Tania was struggling with the “social side of things”.

In these alien environments, Florence, who was privately educated, acted as what Tania called her “pathfinder”. Tania watched how Florence worked a room. She wasn’t comfortable doing the same on her own terms, so she mirrored how Florence “took up space”.

Yet Tania had mixed feelings about this. It had helped her navigate a career in the civil service – she became “posh Tania” at work – but she was troubled by the feeling that the friendship felt contingent on her assimilation. In other words, if she “dropped back down”, Florence might not stick around.

Against the arguments of the original study in Nature, the successful cross-class friendships we studied were not based on one-way transfers. Rather, they relied on a careful negotiation of class difference, which we term “class diplomacy”.

Diplomacy is a useful term, because it shows how managing class difference is an ongoing part of these friendships. It requires significant emotion work (although this burden is not necessarily felt equally) and demands certain social skills from both parties.

We identified three modes of class diplomacy: joking, avoiding and confronting. First, many friends used teasing and self-deprecation to voice and defuse class tensions. Humour was present across genders, but it was more overtly connected to class in male friendships. Typically, it played out in terms of mocking oneself or each other in class terms.

Peter, a banker from a white working-class family, explained the enduring role that “taking the piss” played in his friendship with Julian (“your typical private schoolboy jokes”). What was important, though, was that Julian would take this on the chin. In this way, joking – particularly jokes that punched upwards – recognised class difference but also registered how it affected their experiences in different ways.

The second way diplomacy played out was via the choice many had made to avoid discussing class. Avoidance allowed forms of connection to flourish – interviewees told us these would be stymied if they were to confront class.

But at the same time, interviewees were acutely aware of how class difference continually threatened the friendship. Both friends intricately navigated how and when to coordinate their mutual avoidance.

Many described pivoting to other sources of shared connection such as gender, race, sexuality or taste. This did not cancel out tensions – class “landmines” – yet focusing on commonality provided a kind of refuge.

Others chose to confront class difference head-on. These participants, disproportionately women, acknowledged the risks of this honesty, but said that, if accompanied by sensitivity, it could be productive.

Shanthi and Nadia agreed that their different backgrounds had largely been superseded by the “bonding effect” of being two women of colour growing up in a “very white” area. Yet the issue of money was an ongoing tension.

Nadia, whose upbringing had been marked by economic precarity, was uncomfortable with Shanthi continually offering to buy her things. Shanthi realised that even if her offers were coming from a “place of love”, they almost legitimised a power difference.

Class diplomacy paves the way for forms of exchange and reciprocity to flourish between friends. This is vital for friendships across class to persist. In the relationships we studied, this also had a mutually socialising effect that often led to a heightened sensitivity to class inequality.

Friends spoke of how they had been “shaped” by one another. For those from more advantaged backgrounds, this was often about confronting one’s own class privilege and snobbery – of bringing out, as charity worker Marco noted, “behaviours in me that I’m a bit ashamed of and I’m hyper-aware of now”.

For less privileged friends, diplomacy helped them to understand someone they initially saw only through the lens of privilege, and subsequently be more empathetic, while maintaining their critical stance on class inequality.

These results provide a rejoinder to economists who, in a rush to find a magic bullet to social mobility, may have passed over the complexities of cross-class friendship. It’s not just about the creation of these friendships, but their quality and longevity, and fostering the conditions where they can flourish.

articles.title: How the US power rivalry with Russia and China is turning outer space into the next battlefront
articles.author: Scott Shackelford, Professor of Business Law and Ethics, Indiana University
paras: U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink recently confirmed that the United States has weapons deployed in Earth’s orbit. To date, the U.S. Space Force, the space service branch of the U.S. armed forces, has provided relatively few details about what these weapons are or what they can do except that they are what Meink called “on-orbit space control weapons.”

Meink’s announcement is significant, but not necessarily because the U.S. is the first country to place weapons in orbit. For years, the U.S., Russia and China have accused each other of developing and testing such capabilities, although none has publicly acknowledged deploying space weapons – until now.

We are scholars of space law and governance, and our research illustrates the challenges of uniting diverse groups to establish norms related to the use of resources, safety zones and conflict prevention in new domains such as space. Without better communication and deeper coordination between the world’s space powers, we could witness the beginning of a space arms race.
Failed attempts to prevent a space arms race
In 1981, the United Nations added the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, known as PAROS, to its agenda.
More than four decades of diplomatic efforts under PAROS have produced meager results, though there was a United Nations agreement in 2024 that made progress on reducing threats.

Despite many countries’ proclamations supporting space arms control, no multilateral treaty banning weapons in space has been adopted. With global arms control generally in retreat, and the apparent lack of political will among the three major space powers, efforts to control space weapons have reached an impasse.
The question increasingly is not whether an arms race in space can be prevented, but how it will be managed.
Ambiguities allow weaponization
The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, to which all major space powers are parties, is often described by scholars, practitioners and policymakers as the constitution of outer space.

Article IV of the treaty remains the only legally binding international provision specifically regulating weapons in outer space. The article prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. It also imposes a broader prohibition on military activities on the Moon and other celestial bodies, including establishing military bases, testing weapons and conducting military maneuvers.

However, the article does not prohibit conventional weapons in Earth’s orbit. That omission is significant. The treaty can be understood as implicitly permitting what it does not prohibit: the placement of such weapons in orbit.

China has used these ambiguities as cover for its own space weaponization efforts. In a 2007 test, China destroyed one of its own satellites while in orbit, and it has recently deployed a mysterious space plane.

China, nonetheless, reacted critically to the recent U.S. weapons announcement. In September 2026, it urged Washington to stop expanding its military presence in space. That same month, Russia renewed calls for the demilitarization of outer space.

Both countries have long advocated stronger international restrictions on space weapons. Russia and China twice jointly proposed a treaty prohibiting the placement of weapons in outer space. The U.S. opposed the proposals in 2014, pointing to their failure to also cover important ground-based, anti-satellite weapons.
But Russian and Chinese declarations in favor of keeping weapons out of space sit uneasily alongside their own activities.

In 2020, U.S. Space Command, part of the Defense Department, accused Russia of testing a space-based anti-satellite weapon after an orbiting Russian satellite released a projectile. Russia said the spacecraft was performing an inspection mission.
In 2024, the United States said Russia had launched another satellite, Cosmos 2576, which it assessed to be a “counter space” weapon capable of attacking other satellites.

China has similarly demonstrated increasingly sophisticated operations in orbit. Five Chinese spacecraft conducted satellite flybys in 2024, an exercise that a senior U.S. Space Force officer later described as practicing “dogfighting in space.”

None of this proves that every suspicious Russian or Chinese spacecraft is a weapon. Many technologies used for servicing, inspection and maneuvering around satellites are inherently dual-use. But it does put Moscow’s and Beijing’s calls to keep weapons out of space in perspective.

It also illustrates the security threat now taking shape. Washington can point to Russian and Chinese activities to justify its own weapons. Moscow and Beijing can now point to acknowledged U.S. weapons to help justify their actions, which could result in a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Space has been part of warfare for decades. The 1991 Gulf War has sometimes been called the first “space war” because of the unprecedented role satellites played in navigation, communications, intelligence and targeting. But satellites primarily supported military operations taking place on the ground.
That distinction has gradually eroded. NATO formally recognized space as a military theater in 2019.
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine then demonstrated something different, in which the very definition of a weapon was challenged.

Hours before Russian troops crossed the border, a cyberattack disrupted the U.S. satellite network Viasat, in what was dubbed by commentators as the first “space-cyber war.” Space-based services were no longer merely supporting military operations but were themselves deliberately targeted as part of a military campaign.

The acknowledgment of weapons in orbit represents another step in that evolution. Space assets are transitioning from systems that primarily support warfare in other domains to systems that can be weapons, targets and participants in combat and are often replete with vulnerabilities that could be exploited by an adversary.

That does not mean future space warfare will resemble Star Wars dogfights or Starfleet armadas taking on Borg cubes. But the emerging battlefield is likely to be much more complicated. Satellites can be disrupted through jamming and spoofing, disabled through cyberattacks, approached or manipulated by other spacecraft, attacked from Earth or potentially attacked by weapons already in orbit.

This makes the connection between space and cyberspace particularly important. A country seeking to neutralize an adversary’s satellites may have several options, ranging from a cyberattack or electronic interference to physically damaging it. At the same time, space-based critical infrastructure has never been more vital to the functioning of the global economy.
Military strategy therefore has to adapt not merely to warfare in space but to warfare across an increasingly interconnected space-cyber nexus.
An arms race that must now be managed

The important question is no longer whether space will become militarized. It has been militarized for decades. Nor is it even whether states will develop weapons capable of affecting objects in space. Several already have done so.

The new question is how nations manage a strategic environment in which weapons are openly deployed in orbit, satellites are increasingly being targeted, and attacks can move between the space and cyber domains.
Public acknowledgment may itself have strategic consequences.

The U.S. Space Force argues that revealing the existence of its orbital weapons can strengthen deterrence by making adversaries aware that it possesses capabilities with which to respond. But transparency can also accelerate competition.
Russia and China can now point to U.S. weapons to justify deploying their own. The same logic and its consequences animated debates during the Cold War.

Forty-five years after the United Nations began debating the prevention of an arms race in outer space, that arms race increasingly looks less like something to prevent than something governments must learn to manage.

Scott Shackelford receives funding from the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research to study the nexus of space-cyber power, which will culminate in the publication of an edited volume on this topic. Indiana University is also a member of the Space ISAC.

articles.title: The stunning transformation of the Southern Democratic Party, in one lifetime
articles.author: Gibbs Knotts, Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Two of the biggest surprises of the 2026 election cycle were Democratic U.S. Senate victories in the Deep South. In addition to Annie Andrews’ victory in South Carolina, Scott Colom won a close contest in Mississippi, a place that historian James Cobb called “The Most Southern Place on Earth.”

Colom is not Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator. Two Black Republicans represented the state during Reconstruction, when state legislatures still selected U.S. senators. But Colom is the state’s first popularly elected Black U.S. senator. He is also the first Democrat that Mississippians have sent to the Senate since 1982.

It is tempting to read this change using a familiar political science term: party realignment. But as political scientists who study political campaigns and Southern politics, we see an equally important transformation in the electorate – the people who can cast votes.

Simply put, the Democratic Party in the South was transformed from a party that defended white supremacy and Black disenfranchisement into one in which Black voters became a central constituency. The Democrats who held Mississippi’s Senate seats for the majority of the 20th century were chosen by an electorate built to exclude Black citizens. Colom was elected by a dramatically different electorate and represents a very different Democratic Party.
To understand the magnitude of the change in Mississippi, it helps to look at the Democrats who came before Colom, what they stood for, and the political power they wielded.
Reconstruction and its end

For a brief period after the Civil War, Black Mississippians exercised real political power. They were a majority of the state’s population and, with the right to vote, helped elect the state Legislature that sent Hiram Revels to the U.S. Senate in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875, both of them Black.

That period did not last. White Democrats regained control of Mississippi government in the 1870s, aided by political violence, intimidation and electoral fraud. In 1890, the state adopted a new constitution that used poll taxes, literacy tests and other restrictions to systematically disfranchise Black voters. Two years after the new constitution took effect, the percentage of Black men registered to vote had fallen to just 5.4 percent.

The result fundamentally changed Mississippi politics. For the next several generations, the Democratic Party dominated a political system in which most Black Mississippians had little meaningful voice. Republican electoral victories were rare. One newspaper in 1963 claimed that the election of Lewis McAllister to the state House was the party’s first win in 43 years. Without a competitive general election, winning the Democratic primary often meant winning office, and the politicians who emerged from a one-party system made possible by Black disenfranchisement became some of the most powerful political figures in the state’s history.

What happened in Mississippi reflected a broader pattern across the South. In 1949, political scientist V.O. Key published his seminal study of the region, “Southern Politics in State and Nation.” Key argued that the solid Democratic South rested on systematic disenfranchisement of Black voters.

The one-party system helped keep Black Southerners out of political power while allowing white Southern politicians to present a unified front against efforts to dismantle segregation and expand Black voting rights, particularly when those efforts came from the federal government. Mississippi was among the clearest examples of that system.
Segregation and political power

Before Colom, the last Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi was John Stennis in 1982. He first won election in 1947, filling the seat of Theodore Bilbo, who had won reelection in 1946 after a campaign in which he urged white Mississippians to keep Black voters away from the polls. Stennis won a 1947 special election with 52,068 votes in a state of 2.2 million people. He held that seat for 41 years.

Throughout much of his career, Stennis was an ardent segregationist. In 1956, he was one of 101 members of Congress from the South who signed what was called the “Southern Manifesto.” In that statement, these lawmakers denounced the Supreme Court’s decision in Brown v. Board of Education, in which the justices ruled that the “separate but equal” standards of racial segregation were unconstitutional; Stennis and the other signatories pledged resistance to school desegregation.
Later in his Senate career, Stennis was the only Southern Democrat who voted to oppose the creation of a national holiday honoring Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.

Stennis’ Senate colleague for much of his tenure, Mississippi Democrat James Eastland, was an equally staunch defender of segregation. A cotton planter from the Mississippi Delta, he was appointed to the Senate in 1941 and won the seat outright in 1942. He remained in the Senate until 1978.

The day after the Supreme Court handed down its 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education, Eastland was quoted saying, “the South will not abide by nor obey this legislative decision by a political court.”

Recent attention has understandably focused on Stennis, the last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate. When Colom takes office, he will occupy the Senate seat once held by Eastland and Democrat James Vardaman, who said that “if it is necessary every Negro in the state will be lynched; it will be done to maintain white supremacy.”

One-party rule also gave Mississippi’s senators unusual power. With little electoral competition, they could remain in office for decades. In a Senate where seniority mattered, longevity translated into influence.

Eastland, for example, chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee for more than two decades, giving him enormous influence over civil rights legislation. During his chairmanship of the powerful committee, that committee became known as “the graveyard of civil rights legislation,” according to the Senate’s website.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 helped dismantle the electoral system that had sustained these men in office. Before it, fewer than 10% of Black Mississippians were even registered to vote. Within a few short years, a majority were.

Black voters increasingly aligned with the Democratic Party as its national leaders embraced civil rights, even while many Democratic officeholders in Mississippi continued to defend segregation. That meant Black voters sometimes supported incumbent white segregationists. The party’s voters changed faster than many of its candidates did.

The 1978 election for the seat Colom will hold illustrates how complicated that transition could be. After Eastland retired, Charles Evers, brother of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, ran as an independent and drew nearly a quarter of the vote. His candidacy split the traditionally Democratic vote, helping Republican Thad Cochran win with a mere plurality.
By the 21st century, white Mississippians overwhelmingly supported Republican candidates, and Republican dominance had replaced the old Democratic dominance in most statewide elections.
That pattern made Colom’s victory all the more striking. He won with overwhelming support from Black voters while also attracting enough white voters to build a winning statewide coalition.

The contrast with Mississippi’s old Democratic coalition could hardly be sharper. The Democratic Party of Vardaman, Bilbo, Eastland and Stennis maintained its power in part by keeping Black Mississippians away from the ballot box with violence and Jim Crow laws.
When Colom is sworn in, Revels’ old seat will, for the first time, be held by a Black senator directly elected by Mississippi voters.

articles.title: A Westmoreland County easement shows how landowners can protect farmland without selling it
articles.author: Andrew P. Morriss, Professor of Law, Bush School & School of Law, Texas A&M University; Institute for Humane Studies
paras: Scott Tomlinson still owns the 35 acres in Ligonier Township in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, that his family has cared for over seven generations. But in July 2026, he sold part of what it means to own them.

For US$139,000, Tomlinson gave the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy the right to enforce restrictions on how the land is used, TribLive reported. The restrictions protect its farmland and woods from future development in perpetuity.

According to the report, the property is about 80% forest, with slopes that drain into a tributary of Loyalhanna Creek. It includes habitat for buffalo nut, a shrub the state lists as a rare species of concern, and farm soils the USDA classifies as “farmland of statewide importance.”
That is how a conservation easement works: The land stays privately owned, but its owners agree to limits on what they can do with it.
Such agreements let today’s landowners make conservation decisions that bind future owners.

In more than two decades of studying private land conservation, I have found that deciding which rights to give up, how to pay for conservation and how to handle future changes can be complicated. My family has also spent roughly two years negotiating an easement on our own family’s ranch in Texas.
Dividing the rights of ownership

Think of land ownership as a bundle of sticks, with each stick representing a different property right. Within the limits of the law, owners can build on the land, farm it, subdivide it and more. An easement separates particular rights from the rest of the bundle.

For example, an access easement gives someone else the right to cross your property. In a conservation easement, the landowner voluntarily gives up the right to use the land in specified ways. A land trust or government agency receives the right to enforce those limits.

Imagine someone who owns a 1,000-acre farm that has long been in her family. Development is spreading into the surrounding countryside, and neighboring farms are being divided into smaller properties or subdivisions. She wants her land to stay largely intact. One stick in her bundle is the right to subdivide.

A farmer who grants an easement might agree to limit how many parcels future owners can carve out of the farm while still allowing farming. The farmer could still sell the property or pass it on, but whoever owns it next would also be bound by the restrictions, because the farmer can’t sell rights the farmer no longer owns. Those future owners may have no intention of subdividing. But the farmer who signs the easement can’t know what their children, or someone who buys the farm a century from now, will want to do.

Tomlinson’s worry – that land his family has cared for since the 1870s could be sold off for development once he’s gone – plays out against a broader shift in the county’s farm landscape. According to the USDA Census of Agriculture, Westmoreland County experienced a 10% decline in the total number of farms between 2017 and 2022, dropping from 1,099 to 989 farms, even as total farmland fell only about 4%.

Easements like Tomlinson’s are one way landowners have responded. The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy says it has permanently protected more than 30,000 acres in the Ligonier Valley since the 1970s, more than 12,000 of them through easements.
Negotiating which rights to restrict

Easement terms are negotiated property by property. In my family’s negotiations, we have had to work out what we and future owners can still do with the ranch. We have agreed to limit where future buildings can go, to permanently restrict the use of certain pesticides and to prohibit new roads and stream crossings.
Other easements may allow different agricultural, forestry or construction activities, depending on their terms.

Reaching agreement can be expensive. Natural Lands, a Pennsylvania land trust, lists typical transaction costs. These include surveys, appraisals, environmental assessments, legal fees, title work and documentation of the property’s existing condition. The cost to negotiate my family’s easement has run well into six figures.

Once an easement is signed, the holder is responsible for monitoring and enforcing it for as long as it lasts. Land trusts commonly ask landowners for stewardship funding to help pay for that future work.
The land trust that holds our easement will work with whoever owns the land after us, not just with us, so choosing the right partner was an important part of our decision.
How conservation is financed
Beyond transaction costs, granting an easement usually lowers a property’s market value.

To see how this works, imagine the hypothetical farm is worth $4 million with its development rights and $2 million once an easement sharply restricts subdividing it. (These figures are for illustration; how much an easement lowers a property’s value varies widely with its location, development potential and the restrictions involved.) Appraisers often value an easement by comparing a property’s value before and after it’s placed on the land. Here, the easement would be worth $2 million: the amount it cuts from the property’s value.
To encourage landowners to grant easements, U.S. tax law allows a charitable deduction for donated easements that meet detailed requirements. Easements can also be sold.

In Tomlinson’s case, private foundation grants paid for the conservancy’s purchase. Government programs offer another route: The U.S. Department of Agriculture helps eligible organizations, such as land trusts and state and local governments, to buy easements on farmland. These payments and tax benefits can help landowners absorb the drop in property value. For the public, buying or subsidizing easements can protect more land per dollar than buying land outright.
Tax benefits and tax abuse
The tax breaks tied to easements have also invited abuse.

The Internal Revenue Service has identified inflated appraisals and improperly large charitable deductions as recurring problems. A 2019 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that some promoters sold investors stakes in partnerships and similar entities that then donated easements at inflated values. When appraisals exaggerate a property’s development potential, investors can claim deductions based on those inflated values.
Congress later restricted deductions for certain conservation contributions by partnerships and corporations. Courts have also disallowed deductions and imposed penalties in abusive transactions.
What it means to protect land forever
To qualify for the federal charitable deduction, a donated easement must protect the land permanently.

Property scholar Gerald Korngold of New York Law School has argued that the permanence that makes easements attractive also makes them hard to adjust and that changing ecological conditions and competing community needs can create reasons to revisit restrictions.

In one case Korngold describes, a conservation easement in Vermont blocked the federal government from adding the land to a national wildlife refuge – a move every party supported – because federal rules require clear title.

I have taught property law for decades and have written about the challenges of private land conservation for much of that time. These experiences taught me that an easement has to address two things: what to protect and what happens if circumstances change.

Negotiating one for my family’s ranch made that, and the bundle of sticks metaphor, real for me. We had to write language setting the dimensions of the particular sticks my grandchildren will live with, under conditions none of us can predict.

Done properly, a conservation easement leaves room for land use to adapt without undermining its conservation goals. It lets landowners like Tomlinson’s family and mine protect land while keeping it in private hands.
Andrew P. Morriss is affiliated with Property and Environment Research Center (PERC).

articles.title: Thanksgiving dinner is likely to be served with a side of political disagreement
articles.author: Matthew W. Kreuter, Kahn Family Professor of Public Health, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: Every year as Thanksgiving approaches, news stories are written about how holiday gatherings bring together people who see the world very differently, sometimes leading to uncomfortable dinner conversations. The stories usually include advice about avoiding awkward moments and topics that are off-limits, and navigating heated conversations if they arise.

As experts in health communication and public health, we are keenly aware of how conversations with family members and close friends shape people’s decisions and actions and that sometimes the benefits of having difficult conversations outweigh the potential costs. We wondered how often difficult conversations actually take place at Thanksgiving meals and what the conversations are about.

Although studies have demonstrated that Thanksgiving meals involving people with diverse political viewpoints were shorter by 24 minutes than meals among people holding similar views, we found no estimates of how often these conversations occur.

Our survey of 354 adults from 17 states found that over half – 57% – will share a Thanksgiving meal this year with at least one person from outside their household who sees the world very differently than they do. In 4 out of 5 of these cases, the way their viewpoints differ is politics.

The survey participants were initially recruited to represent differing perspectives on health; they were not randomly selected to represent the general population. That means the survey’s findings may not be generalizable beyond the study sample.
Table talk: What do Americans expect this Thanksgiving?

From Nov. 7-9, 2026, we surveyed 354 adults from 17 states about their plans for this year’s Thanksgiving. Respondents were part of an ongoing health knowledge monitoring and response system. Their mean age was 47.1 years; three-quarters of them were women; and they were racially and ethnically diverse, with 44% white, 33% African American, 15% Hispanic ethnicity and 8% another race or ethnicity. About 1 in 10 were rural residents, and 43% had children under 18 living in their home.
The questions about Thanksgiving meals were sent to 430 people on Nov. 7; 354 completed a survey, which is an 82% response rate.
Of the 354 respondents, 80% expected to share a meal with family members or friends from outside their household during the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday.

Those planning to share a meal with others from outside their household were then asked, “Holiday meals sometimes bring together people from different generations, with different views, or different life experiences. Thinking about your upcoming Thanksgiving meal, will anyone be there who sees the world very differently than you do?”
Almost 71% of those planning to share a meal with others outside their household said yes.

Asked “What are those differences about?” by far the most common response was politics, at 81%, followed by religion at almost 58%, differing views about people such as their career choices or relationships at 54%, health at 53%; and half of the respondents said money. A few mentioned other differences such as “raising children” and “parenting” and “gender expression” and “LGBTQ.”

Asked if they think any of those differences will be expressed during the meal, almost 60% said yes. This was especially true for differences in politics. A large majority – 79% – of respondents said that differences in politics would be expressed during the meal. Fewer respondents – 40% or less – expected that differences in views about people, money, religion or health would be expressed.
Then our questions got to who is expected to disagree – and what respondents anticipate the disagreements will be about. These responses varied by race and ethnicity.

White respondents were more likely than African American or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their Thanksgiving meal will view politics differently from them. African American respondents were more likely than White or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their meal will view money matters differently and were more likely than Hispanics to say that others at their meal will view certain people differently.

In short, it’s highly common for those gathered around any Thanksgiving table this year to have different views on key matters, but the differences you’re most likely to hear about during mealtime conversation are political.

Science tells us that conflict resolution improves through dialogue by reducing stereotypes and changing attitudes that tend to divide people. Holiday meals could provide some clues about how Americans navigate conversations with those who hold different viewpoints from them on politics, religion, money and health.
As one panel member commented: “I don’t keep people around just because they agree with me on something. I don’t cut people away because we disagree about something.”
Tori De La Vega contributed to this story.

articles.title: Expect to see fewer and smaller potatoes this Christmas – it’s the ‘worst harvest since 1950s’
articles.author: Robin Gowers, Senior Lecturer at the Writtle School of Agriculture, Animal and Environmental Sciences, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: Britain’s potato harvest this winter could be one of the smallest in decades.

This is partly down to the hot summer and a poor growing year. Potatoes have shallow roots and need steady moisture, so dry spells cut yield and size. Where farmers had stored water to regularly irrigate, crops fared better.

With 75% of England in drought in September, and Wales also affected by dry conditions, one model estimated that British potato yields would be 11% below average. It used the 2018 harvest as a guide. Some farmers reported a greater than 50% drop in how many potatoes they were harvesting.
Wholesale prices had already risen by more than 40% by early August. By September, big British buyers were reportedly paying more than £300 a tonne for potatoes.
The Food and Drink Federation has warned of the worst potato harvest since the 1950s.

Growers have warned supermarkets to expect smaller potatoes and tighter supplies this year, so shoppers may need to accept wider variation in size and quality. This is partly because other European countries, which often provide supplies to the UK, suffered the same hot summer, and this affected their crops, too.

But shoppers may not feel the full effect of higher wholesale prices this winter. Potatoes are more likely to become significantly more expensive next year. It is also worth noting that many supermarkets subsidise potato prices.

Lidl has announced that a 2kg bag will cost 9p in the week before Christmas. The supermarket says it is funding the low price itself, so this price tells shoppers nothing about what the crop costs to grow.
Supermarkets agree prices and volumes with farmers well in advance. Retailers may absorb some of the higher costs this year rather than risk losing customers to competitors.
The bigger question is whether British farmers will carry on planting Britain’s favourite vegetable in future, and what happens if more decide it is no longer worth the risk.
In 2025, the issue was too many potatoes heading for shops – the UK produced 5.5 million tonnes, 8.5% more than the year before. This caused prices paid to farmers to collapse.

By February 2026, top-quality maris piper potatoes were fetching about £180 a tonne on the open market, less than half the £400 of a year earlier. Contract prices for the following year were also weaker.
Growers did what economics predicts: they planted less. Analysts put this year’s area in Great Britain at around 101,000 hectares, well below the 117,500 recorded in 2020.
Then came the heat and drought.
Why can’t farmers cash in?

Higher prices should encourage farmers to plant more. But a price spike helps only those with potatoes to sell at open-market rates. Most crops are grown under contract, and growers who struggle to deliver the agreed tonnage or quality may miss out.
Some big buyers that normally rely on contracts are buying open-market potatoes as fast as they can, so growers with uncommitted crops may do well.
Meanwhile, costs for farmers keep climbing. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and fertiliser costs. Labour and machinery are also more expensive.

Meanwhile, the end of the basic payment scheme (an annual payment for farmers that followed environmental guidelines) and controversies about its replacements may have removed a financial cushion that once helped farms through bad years.

The potato contract price is fixed in advance, so growers have little room to pass costs on. Tighter margins are also hitting buyers, packers and processors, but it is growers that carry the bulk of the weather risk.

Economists call this pattern the cobweb cycle. In the textbook version, farmers plant according to last season’s price, so a glut leads to a price crash, then cuts in planting, then shortage and high prices, then over-planting again. Potatoes have followed this familiar cycle almost to the letter this year.

Yet several forces pull the other way. Speaking before the summer’s hot weather and drought, in May, Scott Walker, chief executive of the industry body representing the potato sector, GB Potatoes, said that many growers were weighing up how much exposure they would carry into 2027. The body has warned that growers could leave the business or reduce their crop.

Contract prices were weaker this year, costs are higher, and drought has shown how exposed the crop is. Depressed cereal markets offer little alternative income, so a wholesale exit is not certain either.
Farmers will be looking closely at what supermarkets offer them in 2027. High open market prices alone will not bring growers back.

Two things matter most: the contracts offered this winter, and whether farmers can secure water supplies for next summer. Signs are that water access may remain tight. For instance, the Environment Agency put England’s reservoirs at only 54% of capacity in early October. Higher prices could prompt a rebound in planting, but a normal-weather harvest could tip the market back into glut, forcing prices down again.
Will British farmers stop planting potatoes?

In September 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs saw no indication that winter supplies were at risk but added that it was too early to assess the drought’s full impact on potato production and that there was, at that point, no indication that winter potato supplies were at risk. Registered potato farmer numbers fell from about 2,466 in 2000 to 1,611 in 2020, when the statutory body collating data on potato farmers was discontinued. But each bad year pushes more to ask whether the crop is worth it.

Tim Rooke, National Farmers’ Union potato policy group chair, said in 2025 that the UK imports approximately 1 million tonnes of frozen chips a year, because the risk against return on investment of growing potatoes is astronomically high.

A food system that leaves a shrinking number of growers to absorb the weather and price risk should not be surprised when they plant less. One option could be fairer contracts that share risk, and investment in water storage. But less certain supply chains and more volatile prices could cost shoppers more.
Climate change means water shortages and high temperatures will happen more often across Europe. Potato farmers are, therefore, likely to face these challenges more regularly in the future.

articles.title: The UK citizenship test is elitist – it needs an overhaul
articles.author: Anna Tuckett, Senior Lecturer in Anthropology, Brunel University of London
paras: The UK citizenship test – known as the Life in the UK test – was launched in 2005. Since its inception, the test has been mocked for its “pub quiz” style questions, which many people born and raised in the UK struggle to answer.

For thousands of people, the test is what stands between them and a stable, settled life in the UK, as failing it can mean being denied indefinite leave to remain. And while the questions may seem trivial, they highlight a more serious debate about British identity and society.
As the government sets out changes to the country’s settlement and citizenship requirements, a “refresh” of the test has been announced.

The test was first introduced in 2005, during a time of heightened public concern around citizenship, national identity, integration and multiculturalism. However, its current form reflects significant changes made under the Conservative-Liberal Democrats coalition government in 2013.

These included replacing practical information about education, healthcare, policing and neighbourhood safety with historical and “cultural” knowledge. New topics included the Wars of the Roses, Jane Austen novels, the achievements of Sir Francis Drake and major sports events.
The 2013 changes also removed the option to take a language and citizenship course instead of a multiple-choice test, in a bid to toughen up settlement requirements.

While there are no state-funded classes to help candidates prepare for the test, there is an official Life in the UK Handbook. But just reading the handbook is often not enough to pass the test. Those with lower levels of formal education struggle to understand and absorb the handbook’s dense 180-page summary of British values, history, society and politics.
Many therefore turn to privately run training centres which, for a fee, help candidates to prepare. I have conducted long-term ethnographic research in several of these centres across London.
Attendees hailed from many countries, although often from former British colonies. Many had lived in the UK for years, and several had even been to school in the country.

The test’s more practical questions – such as “What is the name of the UK currency?” – were well known by applicants. But much of the handbook’s contents were unfamiliar to them despite many having lived in the country for a long time.
My research found a notable disconnect between the way the handbook and test represent Britishness and the applicants’ everyday experiences in the country.

The Life in the UK test highlights many of the tensions and contradictions that surround the contemporary boundaries of Britishness. Even the handbook’s subtitle – A Guide for New Residents – is discordant. Many of those I met who were taking the test had lived in the UK for decades, and were already well integrated into their local communities.
My respondents may not have been regulars at the local pub, but they all worked, paid taxes, watched popular TV shows, chatted with their neighbours and sent their children to local schools.

Despite being already embedded in everyday British life, many of these people had failed the test, which features questions on roast beef, the Proms, the British monarchy and saints of the middle ages. Applicants had to answer questions such as:

What did St Augustine and St Columba do during the Anglo-Saxon Period? A. They invented new farming techniques B. They led an uprising in Wales C. They helped to spread Christianity across Britain D. They fought courageously against the Romans

Far from signalling a failure of integration, my research shows that these test failures were a product of the handbook’s antiquated, cliched and elitist representation of “Britishness”. The people I spoke to had failed the test because the Britain it presented, which also seemed to equate being British with being white.
A Long and Illustrious History

Perhaps the clearest way in which the UK citizenship test process actively associates Britishness with whiteness is through its account of British history. The handbook chapter titled A Long and Illustrious History focuses on monarchs and battles, and reads like an outdated history textbook.

Reflecting the idea that British identity has ancient roots, the chapter traces British history from the stone age to Brexit and beyond. But this account of the country’s history is more remarkable for what it leaves out than for what it includes.

A group of historians – which includes David Olusoga and Yasmin Khan – have called for a review of the test. They argue that the handbook misrepresents slavery and empire by presenting the abolition of slavery as, in the historians’ words, a “British achievement” in which the enslaved “played no part”, while colonial protests, uprisings and independence movements are missing from the record.

Discussions about the Life in the UK test tend to focus on its trivial content, widely seen as irrelevant to everyday life and unfamiliar even to those who have grown up in the country. But this emphasis on triviality detracts from what many see as the test’s racist and exclusionary message about what constitutes authentic Britishness. The test itself is therefore anything but trivial.

Attempts to control who can be deemed truly British are nothing new. The version of British history and culture presented in the Life in the UK test is just one part of a long history of British nationality and citizenship policy, much of which reflects a desire to equate authentic Britishness with whiteness.

This persistent version of authentic Britishness is not only discriminatory towards immigrants, but also towards many British people, in particular those for whom migration is part of their identity. The citizenship test was, in theory, introduced to produce social cohesion. In its current form it is an expression of a particular ideology of Britishness – one that fosters division and alienation.

articles.title: US foreign policy leaders say America should take an active role in world affairs – but no consensus on whether Trump’s policies are working
articles.author: Joshua Busby, Professor of Public Affairs, The University of Texas at Austin
paras: In the wake of the U.S. midterms, Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the election result. Affordability, Vance pointed out, appeared to be central to voters’ choices, with foreign policy decisions such as the Iran war generating higher fuel prices and rates of inflation. Polling before the election confirmed voters’ concerns – nearly two-thirds of Americans disapproved of President Donald Trump’s foreign policy.
But do foreign policy experts share Americans’ concerns?

To answer that question, the University of Texas at Austin, in partnership with the the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, recently surveyed 449 U.S. foreign policy leaders from the executive branch, Congress, think tanks, interest groups, media and academia.

Their responses matter because as the United States struggles to end the Iran war and navigate the fallout of tariff policies, these experts will be tasked with finding solutions to those pressing problems. These foreign policy experts are also likely to be advising presidential candidates in the run-up to the 2028 elections.
Areas of consensus and disagreement
On some issues, there is a consensus.

We found strong bipartisan agreement on the need for the U.S. to take an active role in the world, the importance of supporting NATO, and the use of force to support European allies if they are attacked.

Ninety-three percent of experts want the United States to take an active part in the world. That includes 83% of Republican experts, 98% of Democrats and 90% of independents. More than 70% of Democrats and more than 80% of Republicans and independents among foreign policy experts we surveyed agree that military power has been very important to American influence in the world. And more than 90% of experts of all partisan stripes agree that economic power has been very important.
However, these points of agreement mask key differences.

On the Iran war, 98% of Democrats and 73% of independent experts say war was the wrong decision, while 58% of Republican leaders say it was correct. While experts of all stripes recognized that tariffs would raise costs for Americans, there were stronger splits on whether tariffs were good for the U.S. economy. One hundred percent of Democrats and 81% of independents say they were bad, while 53% of Republicans say they were good.
These answers largely rally around partisan identities, but responses to philosophical questions about how the U.S. should pursue its interests proved more varied.

The Trump administration has challenged the foundations of U.S. foreign policy through its America First agenda, which favors U.S. domestic and economic interests over international agreements and global alliances.
On tariffs, efforts to expand U.S. territory and the use of force, the Trump administration used coercion to achieve its ends, including with close allies.

The Biden administration used tariffs to counter China’s dominance in areas such as critical minerals and batteries. The Trump administration has applied tariffs to rivals such as China and traditional allies alike, including in Europe and Asia.
The Trump administration also expressed interest in territorial expansion through the acquisition of Greenland and even Canada as a possible 51st state.
Besides military operations to depose and capture the Venezuelan president and war with Iran, the Trump administration has struck boats in the Caribbean suspected of running drugs.

We asked foreign policy leaders to assess the sources of U.S. power and whether there are downsides to a coercive strategy of American dominance. Specifically, we asked them: “In order to achieve U.S. foreign policy goals internationally, do you think it is more important for the U.S. to be feared or admired around the world?”

Sixty-two percent of Republican leaders suggested it is more important to be feared, while 97% of Democrats said it’s more important to be admired. Independents were closer to Democrats, with 81% saying it’s better to be admired.

We also asked whether countries have options to oppose U.S. coercion: “The Trump administration has used coercion, tariffs, punitive sanctions, and threats against many other countries, including traditional allies,” we said. Then we asked, “Which of these best captures your view?”

The respondents had three options to choose from. Thirty-nine percent of Republican experts agreed that “Other countries largely have to accept what the U.S. dictates.” No Democrats and 11% of independents agreed with that sentiment.

Fifty-five percent of Democrats and 54% of independents chose the second option: “Other countries will accept what the U.S. dictates in the short run but will distance themselves from United States order in the longer run.” A large percentage of Republicans – 48% – agreed with that sentiment. This suggests a recognition by Republicans that coercive power alone may have its limits.
A further 44% of Democrats and 35% of independents chose option three, “Other countries have viable options in the short and long run to resist U.S. coercion,” compared to only 13% of Republicans.
These partisan gaps suggest some strong cleavages about the foundations of U.S. power in the world. They also raise questions about how best the U.S. can achieve its interests on the world stage.

A subsequent U.S. president may have to engage in more vigorous dialogue with the American public about the sources of U.S. influence and power. The Trump administration’s coercive turn has some adherents, but many leaders see major costs to that approach and may be open to a new approach to U.S. foreign policy.
Enough damage to the existing world order has been done by the Trump administration, we believe, that a return to establishment internationalism of old is not an option.
Our survey suggests a ripe moment for new ideas and wide-ranging conversation about the U.S. role in the world.
